post:
We renewed every one of our twelve largest hospital contracts this year, and the reason was a staffing decision we made eighteen months ago.

We moved our four strongest area managers off new business and gave each of them three hospital groups to look after full time. It was an unpopular call. New-business numbers dipped for two quarters, and I had to explain that dip in every review.

What the area managers did with the time was simple. They met infection-control teams monthly, not just procurement. They tracked stock-outs on the wards themselves instead of waiting for complaints. When a hospital changed its cleaning protocol, we heard about it before the tender, not after.

The renewals came in at roughly the same prices as last year, which in this market is its own result. Two of the groups have since asked us to quote for sites we had never served.

Most of the credit belongs to those four managers, who gave up commission upside to make this work, and to our regional heads, who backed them.

If you lead institutional sales, how do you protect the time your best people spend on accounts you already have?
why: States a concrete result (all twelve largest contracts renewed at steady prices), owns the unpopular trade-off and gives the credit to the four area managers without inflating it.

post:
Some news I've been sitting on: the transformation programme I designed and led has been named the best digital initiative in UK retail banking at this year's industry awards.

When I took over, the programme was 18 months behind and nobody believed it could be rescued. I rewrote the roadmap in my first fortnight, personally renegotiated every major supplier contract, and set a standard of delivery the organisation had frankly never seen before.

Eighteen months later, we have moved over a million customers onto the new mobile platform, retired three legacy systems and cut journey times in half. I'm told by people who have been in the industry for decades that it's the most ambitious change they've seen a bank pull off.

I don't say this to boast. I say it because I believe it shows what one leader with a clear vision and the courage to make unpopular calls can achieve, even inside a large, traditional institution.

To everyone who doubted it could be done: thank you for the motivation.

If you're leading a transformation and wondering whether you can really move the dial, I'm always happy to share what I've learned. My inbox is open.
why: Claims sole credit for rescuing the programme, quotes praise about himself, uses superlatives ('one leader with a clear vision') and ends with a self-promotional offer.

post:
I'm not sure this is worth a post, and I want to be careful not to overstate anything, because so much of what happens on a project depends on the client, on timing and on factors none of us really control.

We recently wrapped up some work with a distribution client. It was mostly the client's own team who did the heavy lifting, and honestly they probably would have gotten there without us at some point. We helped look at how products were placed in their two main warehouses and suggested some changes to which items sat near the packing stations, though I don't want to claim too much.

Pick rates moved after that, but it's early and it could easily be seasonal, so I'd rather not put a number on it. The client seemed reasonably pleased, I think.

If anything, the main thing I took away was that it's always worth asking a few more questions than you think you need to. That's probably not a new insight for most people reading this.

Anyway, thanks to everyone involved. I'm sure there are many people who could have done this better.

Has anyone else found that?
why: Mentions a real change to warehouse layout and a pick-rate improvement but hedges and disowns it so heavily that the reader cannot tell what was achieved or why it mattered.

post:
Delivering complex infrastructure projects is never easy. It takes vision, discipline and, above all, people.

Over the course of my career, I have learned that success on large projects comes down to a few key principles.

First, safety must always come first. No deadline is worth compromising the wellbeing of the people who build our world.

Second, communication is everything. When everyone is aligned on the goal, teams can achieve extraordinary things.

Third, never stop learning. The industry is constantly evolving, and the best leaders are those who stay curious and embrace change.

Fourth, invest in your people. Your team is your greatest asset, and developing the next generation of site leaders is one of the most rewarding parts of the job.

At the end of the day, infrastructure is about more than concrete and steel. It is about building a better future for the communities we serve.

I am grateful every day to work alongside such talented and dedicated professionals.

Together, we build more than projects. We build legacies.
why: A list of platitudes about safety, communication and people with no project, decision or result; anyone in any industry could have written it.

post:
Our median time from merge to production went from 3 days to 4 hours this quarter.

No new tooling was involved. Most of the delay sat in one place: a manual sign-off step added after an incident in 2022. Nobody on the current team had been there for it.

We replaced the sign-off with two automatic checks: a canary on 5% of traffic for 20 minutes, and an automatic rollback if error rates rise above the baseline. One of our senior engineers wrote the proposal and ran the first 50 releases through it by hand to prove it was safe.

Results after 11 weeks: 214 deployments, 3 automatic rollbacks, zero customer-facing incidents caused by a release. Engineers now ship smaller changes, because shipping is no longer an event.

I approved the change, but the work and the argument belonged to that engineer and the platform team. My contribution was mostly asking what the original sign-off was protecting us from, and accepting the answer.

What process at your company exists because of an incident nobody remembers?
why: Leads with a specific, verifiable improvement, explains the mechanism plainly and credits the engineer and platform team while keeping his own role in proportion.

post:
Today our virtual ward app passed 10,000 patients monitored at home across North Pennine Health Partnership.

When we started, the idea was that patients recovering from heart failure and COPD could send readings from home each morning, and a clinical team would call if anything looked wrong. Simple on paper. In practice we had to redesign the readings screen four times before older patients could use it without a family member helping.

Readmissions within 30 days for patients on the virtual ward are now 14%, against 21% for similar patients who weren't on it. That's hundreds of people who slept in their own beds instead of on a ward.

I'll be honest: there were points when I was the only person in the room who still believed in this. I fought for it through three budget rounds, wrote the business case myself over a Christmas break, and refused to let it be watered down. I genuinely think it's now the best virtual ward service in the country, and I'm incredibly proud that I didn't give up on it.

Thank you to the nursing team who make the calls every morning.

If you're building remote monitoring, what's the hardest part for your patients?
why: Subtle: a credible post with real figures turns boastful in one paragraph claiming she alone believed in it and calling it the best virtual ward service in the country.

post:
This one's a bit of a reflection more than an announcement.

Over the last few months a few of us at Cadence Health have been spending time with care coordinators, trying to understand how they spend their days. It's been a lot of listening, some false starts and plenty of things we got wrong along the way. Honestly, most of the credit goes to the coordinators themselves for putting up with us.

I don't want to make this sound bigger than it is. Product work is mostly small decisions, and most of them are invisible. A lot of what we did was just removing things rather than adding them. Some screens went away. Some steps got merged. It was not glamorous work and I'm not sure it would make for an interesting case study.

There's still so much we haven't figured out, and I'm wary of anyone who claims to have it nailed in healthcare.

Somewhere in there, the average time it takes a coordinator to close out a patient task came down, possibly by around half, but I'd want to see a few more months of data before I'd really say that with any confidence. It might just be that people got used to the tool.

Anyway. Grateful to be learning alongside such a thoughtful team.
why: Subtle: the actual result, coordinator task time roughly halved, is buried in the penultimate paragraph and immediately doubted, so the post reads as a vague reflection.

post:
The future of work is here, and it's hybrid.

As HR leaders, we have a unique opportunity to reimagine how, where and when work gets done. But hybrid work isn't just about flexibility. It's about trust, connection and empowering people to do their best work.

Here are three things I believe every organisation should keep in mind:

1️⃣ Put people first. Engaged employees are productive employees. When people feel valued, they go above and beyond.

2️⃣ Lead with empathy. Every team member has a unique story. Great leaders take the time to listen and understand.

3️⃣ Embrace continuous feedback. The annual review is dead. Regular, meaningful conversations are the key to unlocking potential.

In today's rapidly changing world, the organisations that thrive will be those that put culture at the heart of everything they do.

The question isn't whether hybrid work will succeed. It's whether we, as leaders, are ready to make it succeed.

What do you think? I'd love to hear your thoughts in the comments below! 👇

#FutureOfWork #HybridWork #Leadership #HR #PeopleFirst
why: Buzzwords, emoji bullets and hashtags about hybrid work with no situation, number or example from her own organisation.

post:
Our receivables are down by roughly a fifth since April, and finance did less than half of the work.

The problem looked like a collections problem. When we sat with the sales coordinators, it turned out most overdue invoices were disputed, not ignored: a wrong part number, a missing delivery note, a price that had changed after the purchase order.

So we stopped chasing and started fixing at source. The sales coordinators now check three fields before an invoice goes out. Our credit team calls the customer's accounts payable team within a week of dispatch, not after the due date. Disputes go to one named person on each side instead of a shared inbox.

The plant logistics team made the biggest difference. They began scanning signed delivery notes the same day, which removed the most common reason customers gave for holding payment.

None of this was sophisticated. It did require two departments to agree that an overdue invoice was a shared problem, which took longer than any of the process changes.

I would be interested to hear how others have moved disputes upstream. Where do yours usually start?
why: Gives a clear relative result, explains the root cause and the fix in plain terms, and credits the sales coordinators and plant logistics team without overselling.

post:
Humbled to share that I've been named one of the top wealth advisors in New York for the third year in a row.

When I started in this business, I was told it would take twenty years to earn the trust of multigenerational families. It took me less than half that. Today I advise some of the most prominent business-owning families on the East Coast, many of whom came to me after working with much larger firms.

People often ask what sets my practice apart. I think it's simple: I see things other advisors miss. I've sat across from founders at the most difficult moments of their lives and helped them make decisions that will shape their families for generations. Last month alone I led three succession conversations that other advisors had been unable to move forward for years.

I also take pride in developing the next generation. Several advisors I've mentored are now among the strongest in our region, and I'd like to think they learned from the best.

None of this happens without hard work and a relentless commitment to excellence.

If you're a business owner thinking about what comes next, I'm always open to a conversation.
why: Opens with a humblebrag about an award, ranks himself above other advisors, implies prominent clients and closes by soliciting business.

post:
A small update, for what it's worth.

I've been supporting a founder in the food and beverage space for a few months. I'm conscious that a fractional role is really about helping the in-house team do their best work, so I'd be uncomfortable taking credit for much of anything here.

We spent some time talking to customers. We had a few conversations about what the brand stands for. Some of the messaging on the packaging and website changed a bit as a result, though the team did all of the actual writing, and frankly the founder had most of the instincts already. I was mostly in the background asking questions.

There may have been some movement in repeat purchases since then. It's hard to separate cause and effect with so much else going on, including a new distributor and the time of year, so I genuinely couldn't say whether our work had much to do with it.

I suppose the general point, if there is one, is that it's worth listening to customers. Most people know that already, of course.

Grateful to have been part of it in a small way.
why: Describes repositioning work but gives all the credit away and will not say whether repeat purchases moved, leaving no clear result for the reader.

post:
Compliance is often seen as the department of 'no'. In my experience, the best compliance teams are the department of 'how'.

In the payments industry, the pace of change is relentless. New products, new markets and new risks emerge every day. In this environment, compliance cannot afford to sit on the sidelines. It needs to be a trusted partner to the business, helping teams innovate responsibly while protecting customers and the integrity of the financial system.

That requires a shift in mindset. Compliance professionals need to understand the business as deeply as they understand the rules. They need to communicate clearly, build relationships across functions and focus on outcomes rather than process for its own sake.

It also requires leaders who value compliance as a strategic capability rather than a cost centre. When compliance is involved early, risks are identified sooner, decisions are better informed and customers benefit.

None of this is easy. But the organisations that get it right will be the ones that earn lasting trust from regulators, partners and customers alike.

Compliance done well is not a brake on innovation. It is what makes innovation sustainable.
why: Subtle: on-topic and written in his measured register with a principle at the end, but it makes only general claims about compliance as a partner, with no example from his own work.

post:
Telling a bank that someone has died used to take our customers an average of three branch visits. It now takes one phone call for most families.

The bereavement journey was never anyone's priority because it does not generate revenue. It did generate some of our most painful complaints, often from people writing to us at the worst moment of their lives.

Over nine months, a small team from operations, the contact centre and our digital squad mapped every step. We found eleven handoffs and four separate requests for the same death certificate. We cut the handoffs to three and now ask for the certificate once.

The team also rewrote every letter in the journey, with a bereavement charity reviewing the drafts. That part took longest and mattered most.

Complaints about the journey have fallen by around 60%. More telling, the contact centre team asked to keep the specialist line staffed after the pilot ended.

The legacy systems are still there; we worked around them rather than waiting for a replacement. That was the right trade-off, and I would make it again.

Which journeys in your organisation get ignored because they do not make money?
why: Names a concrete outcome and the trade-off behind it, credits the cross-functional team and the charity, and states the fall in complaints without hype.

post:
Our team just wrapped a twelve-week engagement that cut a consumer goods company's freight costs by about 18%.

The work itself was a good reminder of the basics. We mapped every lane, found that a third of shipments were moving half-empty because of how orders were cut off at the end of each day, and moved the cut-off by two hours. Simple changes, big money.

What made this one different was the client relationship. The CEO called me personally on a Sunday evening to say it was the most valuable piece of work any consultant had ever done for them, and asked me to present directly to their board. I was the only outside advisor in the room, alongside two of the most respected operating partners in private equity.

Honestly, I think it comes down to the fact that I don't do slides for the sake of slides. I tell clients what they need to hear, even when nobody else will.

Credit to the team, of course, for the analysis.

What's the most valuable conversation you've had with a client this year?
why: Subtle: the analysis is described plainly, but the post pivots to the CEO's personal praise, a boardroom name-drop and a dismissive 'credit to the team, of course'.

post:
It has been a busy period on site, and I wanted to share a brief reflection.

Over recent months, there have been a number of changes to how certain activities are planned and sequenced on one of our projects. I should stress that I played only a very small part in this, and that many people contributed in ways that are difficult to describe fully.

Some of the work related to the tunnelling interfaces, and some related to how decisions are passed between the design and construction teams. In both cases the adjustments were modest. It is possible they have helped a little with the programme, although it is too early to draw firm conclusions, and conditions on site vary considerably from month to month.

There were also some observations on safety, which I would prefer not to characterise until the teams have had time to review them properly.

I mention all of this only because it has been a reminder that on large projects, progress is usually made in small steps and by many hands, and that no individual should claim more than their share.

I remain grateful to everyone involved for their patience and professionalism.
why: Refers vaguely to sequencing changes and safety observations without saying what improved, so whatever was achieved is invisible behind caveats.

post:
Great sales teams aren't built overnight.

After many years in sales leadership, I've come to believe that the strongest teams share a few common traits. They are customer-obsessed. They are resilient in the face of rejection. And they never stop learning.

In healthcare sales especially, the stakes are high. Our customers are working under enormous pressure, and they deserve partners who truly understand their challenges. That means listening more than we talk, and adding value in every interaction.

As leaders, our job is to create an environment where people can grow. That means setting clear goals, giving honest feedback and celebrating wins, both big and small. It also means leading by example. Your team will always watch what you do far more closely than they listen to what you say.

Success in sales is not about hitting this quarter's number. It's about building relationships that last for years.

To every sales professional out there grinding through a tough quarter: keep going. Your effort matters more than you know.

What's the one trait you look for when building a sales team?
why: Sales-leadership clichés ('customer-obsessed', 'keep going') with no specific team, hospital, decision or result.

post:
Six months ago, our electronic prescribing pilot had 31% of prescribers using it. Last week it hit 88% across all four sites.

I'd love to say we had a brilliant plan. We didn't. Our first rollout relied on a two-hour training session, and most junior doctors had forgotten it by their next night shift.

What changed things was a group of 14 pharmacists who volunteered to be on the wards during the first fortnight at each site. They showed people the system on real patients, at the moment it mattered, and fed back every frustration to our developers daily. We fixed 47 issues in those weeks, most of them small: a drop-down in the wrong order, a default dose that didn't match local guidelines.

Medication errors reported at the pilot sites fell from 52 in the quarter before go-live to 29 in the most recent quarter. That's the number I care about most.

Thank you to the pharmacy team, and to the clinical informatics group at North Pennine Health Partnership, who answered messages at 2am without complaint.

If you're rolling out clinical software, who are the people already on the wards who could carry it for you?
why: Uses exact before-and-after figures, admits the first rollout failed and credits the pharmacists and informatics team; warm but not self-congratulatory.

post:
Two years ago I joined Cadence Health with a blank whiteboard. Today our platform is used in over 400 clinics and I couldn't be prouder of what I've built.

People ask me how we went from zero to 400 clinics so fast. Honestly? Vision. I saw what clinicians needed before they could articulate it themselves, and I refused to compromise on that vision even when investors and engineers pushed back.

I personally designed the first version of our scheduling tool on a flight to Boston. It's now the most-used feature on the platform. I wrote the product principles every team still follows. I hired every PM on the team, and I'm proud to say they're the best product org in healthtech, full stop.

Was it easy? No. I worked 80-hour weeks for most of the first year. I missed holidays. But that's what it takes to build something that actually changes healthcare.

I've been asked to speak at three major healthtech conferences this fall, which is a nice validation that the industry is noticing what we've done.

If you're a founder building in health and want to know how to scale product the right way, my DMs are open. 🚀
why: Takes personal credit for the platform's growth ('what I've built'), calls his team 'the best product org in healthtech, full stop' and closes with self-promotion.

post:
I've hesitated over whether to write this, as HR results depend so much on the managers who do the real work, and I'm wary of HR teams claiming credit for things that happen on the floor.

Over the past year we have been trying a slightly different approach to how new warehouse supervisors are supported in their first months. Nothing revolutionary. Some peer conversations, a bit more structure around the first ninety days, a few changes to how their managers check in with them. Much of it was borrowed from what individual sites were already doing, so I can't really call it ours.

I've been told that fewer new supervisors are leaving in their first year than before, though I'd be cautious about reading much into it. There are so many factors: the labour market, individual managers, the sites themselves. It could easily be coincidence, and I wouldn't want anyone to think we'd found an answer.

I suppose if there's anything to take from it, it's that small things might matter, sometimes, in some contexts.

Thank you to everyone who has been patient with us while we experiment.
why: A real reduction in first-year attrition among new supervisors is mentioned once, unquantified, and immediately dismissed as possible coincidence.

post:
After over a decade in engineering, here are 5 lessons I wish someone had told me earlier:

1. Code is the easy part. People are the hard part.

2. Technical debt is real debt. Pay it down before it compounds.

3. The best engineers aren't the ones who know everything. They're the ones who never stop learning.

4. Culture eats strategy for breakfast. If your team doesn't feel safe to fail, they'll never innovate.

5. Ship early, ship often. Perfect is the enemy of good.

Engineering leadership is a journey, not a destination. Every day brings new challenges and new opportunities to grow, both as a leader and as a person.

The most important thing I've learned is that great teams aren't built by accident. They're built by leaders who care deeply about their people, invest in their growth and create an environment where everyone can do their best work.

What would you add to this list? Drop your lessons in the comments. 👇

#EngineeringLeadership #Leadership #SoftwareEngineering #TechLeadership #Growth
why: A familiar listicle of engineering maxims ('culture eats strategy for breakfast') with no number, system or example from his teams.

post:
This year, most of the families I work with brought their adult children to at least one planning meeting. Two years ago, very few did.

It started with a mistake. A client passed away unexpectedly, and his children met me for the first time after the funeral. They had no idea what the plan was or why it had been built that way. Several decisions that made sense to their father looked arbitrary to them.

Since then, I ask every family the same question at the annual review: who would need to understand this plan if you could not explain it yourself? Then I suggest inviting them.

The meetings are slower. Some are uncomfortable. But the conversations have changed what we plan for, and two of the junior advisors on our team now run the follow-up sessions with the next generation themselves, which they do better than I would.

I do not measure this in any report. I measure it by how few surprises families face when something changes.

How do you bring the next generation into the conversation before it is urgent?
why: Describes a specific practice and its observable effect in measured terms, admits the mistake that prompted it, credits junior advisors and makes no performance claims.

post:
I don't usually post about client results, but I've been asked so many times this month that I feel I should.

Since I started working with a regional property developer last year, their enquiries have tripled, cost per lead has fallen by about 60%, and their latest launch sold out in eleven days. The founder told me I'd done more for the brand in nine months than their previous three agencies managed in five years.

I don't think there's any secret. I've simply spent fifteen years learning what most marketers never bother to: how to find the one thing a customer actually cares about and say it better than anyone else. I'm lucky that founders across the region seem to have noticed. My diary for next year is already almost full, and I've had to turn away two major hospitality groups this quarter.

I'm also incredibly humbled to have been asked to judge this year's regional marketing awards alongside some of the most respected names in the industry.

If you're a founder who's tired of agencies that don't deliver, I may have one or two slots left for early next year.
why: A humblebrag ('I don't usually post') that quotes a founder's praise, boasts about a full diary and turned-away clients, and ends with a sales pitch.

post:
A short note, mostly to thank some colleagues.

Over the past few months our compliance team at Lumen Pay has been involved in some work with the product teams on how certain customer checks are carried out. I should be careful here: the product teams did most of the real work, and compliance's contribution was largely to answer questions when asked.

There have been some changes to the order in which information is requested from customers, and a few steps that seemed redundant were reviewed. I would not want to overstate the effect of any of this. Some indicators may have moved in a helpful direction, but I am conscious that many other things changed over the same period, and it would be wrong to draw conclusions from a few months of data.

It is also entirely possible that we have simply been fortunate.

I mention it only because it has been a useful reminder, at least for me, that compliance teams can sometimes be helpful when involved earlier, though I recognise many colleagues in the industry already work this way and have done so for far longer.

Compliance is a team effort, and modesty is usually the right posture.
why: Alludes to changes in customer checks and 'some indicators' moving but never states what improved or by how much, and attributes any gain to luck.

post:
Finance is no longer just about the numbers.

The role of the finance function has changed dramatically in recent years. Today, finance teams are expected to be strategic partners to the business, providing insights that drive better decisions across every part of the organisation.

That shift brings both challenges and opportunities. It requires finance professionals to build new skills, from data analysis to stakeholder management. It requires closer collaboration with operations, sales and procurement. And it requires a mindset that looks forward as much as it looks back.

In manufacturing, where margins are tight and conditions can change quickly, this partnership matters more than ever. The finance teams that add the most value are the ones that understand how the business really works, on the shop floor as well as in the boardroom.

Of course, the fundamentals still matter. Accurate reporting, strong controls and a timely close remain the foundation of everything we do. But they are the starting point, not the destination.

The future of finance belongs to those who can combine rigour with curiosity.

How is the role of finance changing in your organisation?
why: Subtle: polished commentary on finance as a business partner, pitched at her industry, that never mentions a single thing her team actually did.

post:
We helped a consumer goods client release about $40 million of inventory this year without a single new system.

The starting assumption was that their forecasting was poor. It wasn't. The forecast was reasonable; the problem was that each of their six regional planners added their own safety buffer on top of the central one. Nobody had ever added the buffers up.

An associate on our team spent two weeks sitting with the planners and rebuilding their spreadsheets line by line. She found that the combined buffers covered almost five extra weeks of demand on their slowest-moving products.

We didn't recommend replacing anyone or buying software. We recommended one shared safety-stock rule, a monthly review where planners could argue for exceptions, and a simple report showing the total buffer by region.

The client's planning director ran the change himself. Service levels held steady through peak season, which was the real test.

The analysis was not complex. What made it work was someone willing to sit with the people closest to the numbers and ask why.

When did a simple question uncover your biggest finding?
why: States the result plainly, explains how a simple finding produced it and credits the associate and the client's planning director.

post:
I am proud to announce that the interchange project I have led for the past three years has reached substantial completion, well ahead of programme and comfortably under budget.

When I was appointed, the project was significantly behind schedule and many in the industry believed it could not be recovered. I restructured the delivery organisation within my first month, introduced a planning discipline that had not existed before, and personally led the negotiations that resolved the most difficult interface issues with the utilities.

The result is one of the most complex road structures in the region, completed with an outstanding safety record, which I believe is a direct reflection of the standards I set from day one. Senior figures across the sector have described it to me as a benchmark for how such projects should be delivered.

I have always believed that a project reflects its leader. This one reflects the discipline, rigour and determination I bring to every assignment.

I would like to thank the team for following my lead, and I look forward to bringing the same results to the next challenge.
why: Formal in tone but claims sole credit for the recovery and the safety record, quotes praise from senior figures and thanks the team for 'following my lead'.

post:
Some weeks are quieter than others, and this was not one of them.

Our team in the south has been working on a hospital network opportunity since the start of the year. I won't say much about it, partly because the credit belongs entirely to the area managers involved, and partly because I am never comfortable talking about outcomes in public. Whatever happened was down to them.

What I will say is that the process taught me something about patience. There were months with very little visible progress. There were trial periods on wards that seemed to go nowhere, and feedback sessions where we were not sure anyone was listening.

At some point the hospital network made a decision, and it seems to have gone reasonably well for us, though of course these things are never final until they are, and I would not want to tempt fate by saying more.

I suppose the lesson, if there is one, is that institutional sales rewards persistence, though I am sure most people in this field know that better than I do.

How do you keep a team motivated through a long sales cycle?
why: Hints that a long hospital-network pursuit 'went reasonably well' but never says what was won or how big it was, so the reader cannot tell what happened.

post:
Digital transformation isn't about technology. It's about people.

Too many organisations treat transformation as a technology project. They invest in new platforms, new tools and new systems, and then wonder why nothing really changes. The truth is that lasting change only happens when people change how they work.

In financial services, the challenge is even greater. We operate in a complex, highly regulated environment, often with legacy systems that have been in place for decades. Customers' expectations are rising every day, shaped by the best digital experiences they have anywhere in their lives.

So what does it take to succeed? In my experience, it comes down to three things: a clear vision that everyone understands, leaders who are willing to model the change themselves, and a relentless focus on the customer.

Transformation is a marathon, not a sprint. There will be setbacks along the way. But organisations that stay the course, keep learning and put their customers at the centre of every decision will be the ones that thrive in the years ahead.

The best time to start was yesterday. The next best time is today.

What's the biggest barrier to transformation in your organisation?
why: Transformation clichés ('a marathon, not a sprint', 'the best time to start was yesterday') with no programme, decision or outcome.

post:
We shipped our new referral workflow at Cadence Health last month, six weeks later than I promised. Here's why I'm glad we waited.

The original plan had clinic staff filling out referrals on one screen. In testing with front-desk teams at three clinics, we watched them keep a sticky note next to the monitor with insurance details they had to retype from another system. Every single one of them.

So we pushed the launch and built a lookup that pulls that data in automatically. It cost us a quarter's worth of roadmap and a few uncomfortable conversations with our sales team, who had customers waiting.

Early numbers: average time to complete a referral dropped from about 9 minutes to under 4, and the share of referrals sent back for missing information is down by roughly half.

Huge credit to our design researcher, who caught the sticky notes, and to the two engineers who rebuilt the integration in a month.

Lesson for me: a launch date is a promise to your team, but a broken workflow is a promise to the people who'll use it every day.

What's the last launch you delayed, and do you regret it?
why: Admits a missed deadline, gives concrete before-and-after numbers and credits the researcher and engineers; energetic without bragging.

post:
Our regional office moved to a hybrid model eighteen months ago. Last week our engagement survey came back with the highest scores we've ever recorded, and voluntary attrition among office staff is down by about a third.

A few things made the difference. Each team agreed its own anchor days instead of following a regional rule. Managers had a short monthly check-in with each person about workload, not attendance. And we stopped reporting time in the office on the leadership dashboard altogether.

I should say plainly that this was my initiative from start to finish. I single-handedly designed the policy, persuaded a sceptical leadership team and personally coached more than forty managers through the change. Several CHROs I respect have told me it's the most thoughtful hybrid model they've seen in Asia, and I've been invited to present it at two regional HR conferences this autumn.

Hybrid work is not a policy question; it is a trust question. Teams will usually tell you what works if you let them.

What has made hybrid work for your teams?

I've been thinking a lot lately about why some digital projects in healthcare succeed and others don't.

The answer, I think, is surprisingly simple: the ones that work are built with clinicians, not for them.

Our clinical colleagues are the experts in their own work. They know what slows them down, what frustrates them and what would make a real difference to the care they give. When we involve them from the very beginning, we build better tools. When we don't, we build things nobody uses.

It sounds obvious, but it's easy to forget when budgets are tight and deadlines are looming. It takes humility to admit that we don't have all the answers, and courage to change course when something isn't working.

I've learned so much from the incredible nurses, doctors and allied health professionals I've had the privilege of working alongside. Their passion for their patients inspires me every single day.

Digital health has the power to transform care, but only if we keep people at the heart of everything we do. 💙

why: Subtle: warm and close to her voice, but it offers only general sentiments about involving clinicians, with no project, figure or story of her own.

A boutique hotel group I work with now takes about 45% of its bookings direct, up from 20% eighteen months ago.

When I started, the brief was to cut what they paid booking platforms. The team assumed they needed a bigger advertising budget. The research said otherwise.

We interviewed thirty recent guests. Almost none of them had chosen the hotel because of price. They chose it because of the rooftop breakfast and because the staff remembered their names. None of that appeared on the website, which led with room rates and a generic photo of the pool.

So we rebuilt the site around those two things, added a simple returning-guest rate, and trained the front-desk team to mention it at check-out. The marketing manager ran the whole programme; I mostly asked questions and pushed back on the agency's first draft.

Advertising spend actually came down slightly over the period.

The lesson I keep relearning: guests will tell you why they came back if you ask. Most brands are too busy talking to listen.

When did your customers last tell you something you weren't putting in your marketing?
why: Opens with a clear result, shows the research insight that drove it and gives the client's marketing manager the credit for running the programme.

Last month our team handed over the main viaduct structure several weeks ahead of the baseline programme, with no lost-time incidents across the whole elevated section.

Two decisions made the difference, and neither was mine alone.

The first was to move precast segment production closer to the alignment. Our logistics manager argued for it early, when it looked like an unnecessary cost. It cut transport time sharply and removed most of the night-time road closures we had planned for.

The second was a daily lift-planning meeting led by the crane supervisors themselves, not by engineering. They knew which lifts were marginal in the afternoon wind and rescheduled them without waiting for approval. Productivity went up because fewer lifts were abandoned halfway.

Our safety record on this section is the result of hundreds of supervisors and operatives making careful choices every shift. My role was mostly to protect their time and to say yes when they asked for something sensible.

I am grateful to the site leaders who carried this work through a difficult summer, and to the client's engineers, who made decisions quickly when we needed them.

The past few years have taught every supply chain leader the same lesson: resilience is no longer optional.

Disruption has become the new normal. Organizations that once optimized purely for cost are now rethinking their networks, their supplier relationships and their approach to risk. The winners will be those who can balance efficiency with agility.

In my work with operations leaders, I see three priorities rising to the top. First, visibility: you can't manage what you can't see, and end-to-end data is now a competitive advantage. Second, collaboration: the strongest supply chains are built on trust between partners, not just contracts. Third, talent: technology is important, but it's people who turn data into decisions.

None of this is easy. Transformation takes time, investment and leadership commitment. But the cost of standing still is far greater than the cost of change.

The supply chains of tomorrow will be smarter, more connected and more sustainable. The question is whether your organization will lead that change or be forced to react to it.

What's your top supply chain priority for the year ahead?

Two years ago, about a third of our warehouse supervisor roles in the region were filled from inside. This year it was close to two thirds.

The change started with an awkward finding. Our best forklift operators and pickers were not applying for supervisor roles, because the job description asked for a diploma most of them did not have, and the interview panels were mostly people they had never met.

We removed the diploma requirement, added a six-week trial in which interested team members shadow a supervisor for two shifts a week, and put a site supervisor on every interview panel. The site operations managers designed the trial themselves; HR mainly kept the paperwork out of their way.

Internal promotions have stayed in their roles longer than external hires, and the sites with the most internal supervisors now have noticeably lower first-year attrition among their teams.

It was not free. Sites lost productive operators to the trial for six weeks at a time, and two countries pushed back hard before agreeing.

My takeaway: the barrier to growing your own leaders is often a line in a job description that nobody has questioned in years.
why: Gives a clear before-and-after result, explains what changed and what it cost, and credits the site operations managers who designed the trial.

Merchant onboarding at Lumen Pay used to take around twelve working days. It now takes about four, and our risk standards have not moved.

Most of the delay was not in the checks themselves. It was in the waiting between them. A file went from the sales team to onboarding to compliance and back again, often three times, because each team asked for documents the others had already collected.

Our compliance analysts mapped every request and found that a third of them were duplicates. We built one checklist that sales now completes with the merchant at the first meeting, and gave the onboarding team authority to approve standard low-risk cases without a compliance sign-off.

The higher-risk cases still come to us, and they now get more attention, not less, because we are not spending our days on routine files.

Credit to the compliance analyst who led the mapping, and to the head of sales, who agreed to make his team responsible for a checklist they had never been measured on.

Speed and control are rarely in conflict. Duplication is usually what slows both down.

The plant teams adapted well once the framework was in place, and the board pack has gone out on time every month this year.

For me, the lesson is that a finance function performs at the level of the standards its leader sets.

Your brand is not your logo. It is the promise you make and keep.

In a crowded market, it has never been more important for consumer brands to stand for something. Customers today have endless choice, and they are drawn to brands that feel authentic, consistent and true to their values.

Yet so many growing businesses lose sight of this as they scale. They chase every opportunity, speak to every audience and end up saying nothing memorable at all.

The brands that win are the ones with clarity. They know exactly who they serve, what problem they solve and why it matters. Every touchpoint, from the website to the customer service call, reinforces the same message.

Getting there takes discipline. It means saying no to good ideas so you can say yes to great ones. It means listening to your customers more than you talk to them. And it means building a marketing team that understands the brand as deeply as the founder does.

Positioning is not a one-off exercise. It is a habit.

I was not sure this would work, so I waited a year before writing about it.

Last April we stopped allowing area managers to offer discounts above 5% without a written case reviewed by the regional head. Several of our people saw it as a lack of trust, and I understand why.

Twelve months on, our average discount has fallen from around 14% to around 8%, and we lost only two accounts we believe left on price. Gross margin in the institutional business is up by about three points.

The written case turned out to matter more than the approval. Once managers had to explain why a hospital needed a lower price, many of them found a different answer: a training visit for ward staff, a change to delivery frequency, a smaller pack size that cut waste. Those answers held better than discounts did.

I underestimated how much our regional heads would carry. They reviewed hundreds of cases and turned most of them into coaching conversations rather than refusals.

I am still adjusting the threshold, and I expect we will get some of it wrong again this year.

How do you keep discounting honest without taking judgement away from your field teams?
why: Subtle: the tone is cautious, but the result (lower discounts, higher margin) is stated clearly with figures and credit goes to the regional heads, so it reads as confident rather than too modest.

We switched off our last mainframe batch job for current accounts last weekend, after nearly two years of migration work.

The technical work was hard, but the bigger challenge was confidence. Every previous attempt had stalled because nobody wanted to be the person who signed off the cut-over. So we ran the old and new systems in parallel for four months, reconciled every overnight run and published the differences to the whole programme, good or bad.

By the end, the differences were down to a handful a week, all explained. The cut-over itself took six hours, and customers noticed nothing.

I'll admit I'm proud of this one. Frankly, the programme had been through three leaders before me, and it was only when I took it over that it finally started moving. Several people on the executive committee have told me they doubt anyone else could have got it over the line.

Thanks to the engineering and operations teams for their hard work along the way.

Safety is not a priority. It is a value.

Priorities change from day to day, depending on the demands of the programme, the weather or the client. Values do not. On every project I have been part of, the sites with the strongest safety performance have been those where safety is treated as part of who we are, not something we do when someone is watching.

Building that culture takes time. It requires leaders who are visible on site and who listen more than they speak. It requires supervisors who are empowered to stop work when something does not look right. And it requires every worker to feel that their voice matters, regardless of their role or background.

Procedures and training are essential, but they are not enough on their own. Culture is shaped by thousands of small decisions made every day, often when nobody is looking.

As our industry continues to deliver ever larger and more complex projects, our commitment to bringing everyone home safely must remain constant.

Every person on site deserves to return home to their family at the end of each shift. That is the standard we must all hold ourselves to.

In January I made the call to pause feature work for six weeks on our two busiest services. It was the least popular decision I made this year.

We were missing our availability target every month. Customers had stopped raising tickets about it, which worried me more than the tickets had.

During the pause, the two teams fixed what they had been asking to fix for a year: a connection pool that leaked under load, retries that turned small outages into big ones, and a deploy process with no automatic rollback. They chose the list; I protected the six weeks from roadmap pressure.

Availability on both services has been 99.95% or better for seven straight months, up from an average of 99.6% last year. Pages outside working hours fell from 38 a month to 9.

The cost was real. Two features slipped a quarter, and I had to explain that to sales and to two large customers myself.

post:
Frontline leaders are the backbone of every organisation.

They are the people who turn strategy into action, every shift, every day. They set the tone for their teams, solve problems before they escalate and often carry the weight of decisions made far away from the floor. Yet in many organisations, they receive the least investment in their development.

That needs to change. If we want engaged teams, safer workplaces and better results, we need to start by supporting the people who lead them most directly.

In my experience, the most effective development for frontline leaders is practical, relevant and ongoing. It focuses on real situations they face, from difficult conversations to managing change. It gives them space to learn from each other, not just from HR. And it recognises that leadership is a skill that can be learned, not a talent people are born with.

Investing in frontline leaders is not just the right thing to do. It is one of the smartest business decisions any organisation can make.

This year's statutory audit closed with no adjustments to inventory for the first time in at least five years.

Inventory was always where the audit ran long. Each of our four plants valued slow-moving stock in its own way, and every year the auditors found differences we then spent weeks explaining.

Last summer, the plant finance leads agreed one method for identifying and providing for slow-moving items, with clear ageing bands and a monthly review signed off by operations. It sounds administrative. It took six months of argument, mostly about which parts were genuinely obsolete and which were spares a production manager wanted to keep.

The audit fieldwork on inventory took roughly half as long as last year. More useful for the business, we now see provisioning movements every month rather than discovering them at year-end.

The credit belongs to the plant finance leads, who gave up their own methods, and to two production managers who sat through every review and argued their case with evidence.

I am now looking at receivables and fixed assets with the same question: where are we doing the same thing four different ways?

In today's fast-moving fintech landscape, building a world-class compliance team has never been more important, or more challenging.

The regulatory environment continues to evolve. Customer expectations continue to rise. And the line between innovation and risk has never been thinner. Against this backdrop, compliance leaders must do more than keep up. They must lead.

Over the years, I have found that the strongest compliance teams have a few things in common. They hire for judgement as well as knowledge. They invest in continuous learning, because yesterday's rules are rarely enough for tomorrow's products. They communicate in plain language, so that colleagues across the business understand not just what to do, but why. And they build genuine partnerships with product, technology and operations, rather than working in isolation.

Above all, great compliance teams are built on a culture of integrity, where doing the right thing is simply how work gets done.

The future of payments will be shaped by those who can balance innovation with responsibility. That balance starts with the right people.

Integrity is not a policy. It is a practice.
why: Opens with 'In today's fast-moving fintech landscape' and lists generic traits of good compliance teams without a single specific from his own team.
